chicken-drumstick-fried-coated-skin-coat.title: Chicken drumstick, fried, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the meat from the lower leg of a chicken, commonly prepared by frying or baking. When coated and fried, the skin and coating are usually removed before eating, leaving only the lean meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple in both Asian and American comfort foods.
Frying in a breaded coating creates a crunchy crust, but most of the added calories come from oil absorbed into the coating.
Poultry meat is a good source of protein and B‑vitamins.
In many cuisines, drumsticks are served with dipping sauces that enhance flavor.
Drumsticks can be prepared at home or produced on an industrial scale.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Chicken drumsticks contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: They are rich in niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Reduced calories when skin is removed
items.content: Removing the skin and coating lowers the calorie count, beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Fat content in the coating
items.content: Fried breading absorbs oil, increasing total fat and calories, which may be undesirable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Raw chicken can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; thorough cooking is essential.

items.title: Sodium in prepared coatings
items.content: Pre‑made breading mixes often contain added salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken drumsticks can be fried, baked, or grilled. After cooking, the skin and coating are typically peeled off, and the meat can be added to salads, soups, stews, or served as a protein side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw drumsticks in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked fried drumsticks keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or can be frozen for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Dragon fruit (pitaya) is a brightly colored fruit of the cactus genus Hylocereus, native to Central and South America and now cultivated in tropical regions of Asia, Africa and Oceania. The fruit has a mildly sweet flavor reminiscent of kiwi and pear, with crunchy juicy flesh and tiny edible seeds.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The skin can be vivid red, pink, yellow or white depending on the variety.
The tiny black seeds are edible and rich in healthy fatty acids.
Fruits develop after nocturnal pollination by bats and hummingbirds.
In Asian traditional medicine the fruit is used to aid digestion and boost immunity.
Harvest season typically runs from June to September in the Northern Hemisphere.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One fruit provides over 30 % of the daily recommended vitamin C, supporting immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and betacyanins in the flesh help neutralize free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber and water content promote regular bowel movements and help prevent constipation.

items.title: Source of magnesium and iron
items.content: These minerals contribute to muscle function, nerve signaling and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: A medium fruit contains about 60 kcal, making it a suitable option for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to the seeds or flesh of dragon fruit.

items.title: Gastrointestinal issues
items.content: High fiber intake can cause bloating or diarrhea in sensitive people.

items.title: Pesticide residue
items.content: When buying non‑certified fruit, wash thoroughly as it may have been treated with chemicals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the fruit in half, scoop out the flesh with a spoon or dice it. Eat it fresh, add to smoothies, fruit salads, desserts, or use as a decorative element in cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dragon fruit in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer for up to 5 days. At room temperature it stays fresh for 2–3 days. Keep it away from strongly scented foods as it readily absorbs odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Lettuce (Lactuca sativa) is a leafy vegetable usually eaten raw, but it can also be steamed, sautéed, or baked. Heat softens the leaves and gives them a milder, slightly nutty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lettuce belongs to the Asteraceae family and has over 100 varieties differing in taste, color, and leaf texture.
Heat preserves most nutrients, but vitamin C degrades with prolonged cooking.
Lettuce is cultivated in more than 100 countries, with China, the USA, and India being the top producers.
Leaf cells contain small amounts of xylem that, when heated, release aromatic compounds giving a subtle nutty note.
Lettuce is frequently used in Asian cuisine for soups and stir‑fry dishes.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Cooked lettuce retains a good amount of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate supports DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Leaves are rich in carotenoids and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Even after cooking, lettuce remains low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber in lettuce promotes healthy bowel function and gut microbiota.

items.title: Vitamin C loss
items.content: Vitamin C is heat‑sensitive, so prolonged cooking markedly reduces its content.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: If lettuce is not thoroughly washed before cooking, pathogens such as E. coli may persist.

items.title: Asteraceae allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to lettuce components.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Lettuce contains oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked lettuce can be added to soups, stews, omelets, or used as a filling for wraps. It also works well lightly sautéed with garlic and olive oil as a side dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked lettuce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Allow it to cool completely before sealing to prevent moisture buildup.

content.title: About
content.content: Margarine in a tub is a vegetable fat made from refined plant oils, emulsified with water and fortified with vitamins A and D. It has a soft consistency, is easy to use, and is suitable for baking, frying, and spreading on bread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial margarine was created in 1869 in Paris as a cheaper alternative to butter.
Modern margarine often uses oils high in oleic acid, making it a healthier alternative to traditional spreads.
Tub packaging allows the product to be stored at room temperature without the risk of the container cracking.
Emulsifiers such as lecithin are added to improve texture and stability.
Margarine can be enriched with omega‑3 fatty acids and phytosterols to support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and D
items.content: Fortified margarine provides vitamins essential for vision, immune function, and bone health.

items.title: Contains unsaturated fats
items.content: Plant oils in margarine are rich in mono‑ and polyunsaturated fatty acids, which can help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: Current manufacturing processes virtually eliminate trans fats, making the product safer for the heart.

items.title: Convenient to use
items.content: The soft tub texture makes spreading and portioning easy without needing to soften the product.

items.title: Provides energy
items.content: Margarine is a dense source of calories, useful for people with high energy demands.

items.title: Allergy to plant oils
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy or sunflower oils used in margarine.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Margarine is calorie‑dense, so it should be consumed in moderation, especially when managing weight.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Certain varieties contain added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Additive concerns
items.content: The formulation may include artificial flavors and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Margarine in a tub is ideal for spreading on bread, making dough for cookies, cakes and pastries, and for sautéing vegetables or meat. It can be melted and added to sauces for a creamy texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the tub in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 3–4 weeks. Discard if a rancid odor develops.

pizza-cheese-whole-wheat-thin-crust.title: Cheese Pizza, Whole Wheat Thin Crust

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese pizza on a whole wheat thin crust combines a crisp, slightly nutty base made from whole grain wheat with melted cheese, usually mozzarella or cheddar. The pizza provides carbohydrates from whole grain, protein and calcium from cheese, and a modest amount of fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole wheat crust contains more fiber and micronutrients than a traditional white crust.
Thin crust bakes quickly, preserving the bright flavors of the toppings.
Cheese forms a golden, bubbly layer that enhances aroma and texture.
In Italy, whole grain pizza is called "pizza integrale" and is popular in health‑focused eateries.
The combination of whole grain and cheese offers longer satiety compared with plain white‑crust pizza.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole wheat flour provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheese is a good source of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Cheese supplies high‑quality animal protein that aids tissue repair.

items.title: Lower glycemic index
items.content: Whole wheat crust has a lower glycemic index than white crust, helping to stabilize blood sugar.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole wheat and cheese contain B1, B2, and B6 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy allergies or lactose intolerance.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese often adds a lot of salt; choose reduced‑sodium varieties if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: The combination of crust and cheese makes the pizza energy‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Whole wheat crust contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the pizza hot, straight from the oven, or let it cool slightly so the crust stays crisp. Slice into bite‑size pieces and serve with fresh salads, tomato sauce, or herbs for added flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in an oven or skillet to retain crust crispness; avoid microwaving.
